tagline: Across plains and mountain passes, a trading trail becomes a byway.
intro: The Santa Fe Trail byway links plains with mountain crossings across Colorado and New Mexico. Colorado’s 188-mile portion takes four hours to drive in the state transportation department’s account; the full two-state byway totals 565 miles. Designated a National Scenic Byway in 1998, the route is presented by Colorado as a journey through the cultural legacies of an old trade corridor.

The wagon trail connected Missouri with Santa Fe, then a provincial capital of Mexico. William Becknell and Joseph R. Walker pioneered it in 1821. Trade sustained it, but the route also served invasion: the U.S. Army used the trail to enter New Mexico during the Mexican–American War in 1846. The railroad reached Santa Fe in 1880, ending almost 60 years of wagon caravans, as New Mexico’s tourism department recounts.

Drive west through Lamar to La Junta on US 50, then southwest on US 350 to Trinidad. I-25 crosses Raton Pass into New Mexico. The Mountain Branch continues through Cimarron; the separate Cimarron Cutoff comes west from Clayton past the Rabbit Ear Mountains toward Wagon Mound. The branches met at Watrous. Beyond lie Fort Union, Las Vegas and Pecos, with a granite trail-end marker on Santa Fe Plaza.

moments.title: Bent's Old Fort
moments.text: The fort here is a 1976 reconstruction of an adobe trading post built in 1833. Charles and William Bent and Ceran St. Vrain’s company built the original to trade for buffalo robes with Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho people and with trappers. Travelers replenished food and water and repaired wagons here; Kit Carson worked as a hunter for the Bents in 1841. William Bent abandoned the original post in 1849. The reconstruction drew on excavations, paintings, sketches and diaries, but also involved significant guesswork. It is an interpretation of the earlier fort’s form.

moments.title: St. James Hotel, Cimarron
moments.text: The dining-room ceiling at the St. James holds some twenty bullet holes, a surviving detail in a hotel listed in the National Register of Historic Places. When Henry Lambert’s sons replaced the roof in 1901, they found many more holes above. The property later fell into disrepair as railroad transport displaced trail traffic and local gold dwindled. After decades of changing owners, a restoration followed in 1985. It belongs to the Cimarron Historic District in the town’s historic downtown.

moments.title: Fort Union
moments.text: Wagon ruts from both the Mountain and Cimarron branches are visible at Fort Union and along its approach road. The site preserves three successive forts, the first begun in August 1851. Its role as a military supply depot eventually employed more men than its military operations, many of them civilians. Rail transport overtook the trail’s commercial role in 1879; the fort was abandoned in 1891. A self-guiding trail runs through the second and third forts’ remains. Across the valley to the west, the ordnance-depot ruins and the first fort’s site are also visible.
moments.notice: Wagon ruts from both trail branches are visible at the fort and beside the approach road.
